notes.text: Note: Buying prices are for coins in Very Good (VG) condition. Coins of lower grades will be bought at lower prices.
Note: Original wrapped rolls from 1968 to date command a premium over the spending value.
Note: Victoria, Edward and George V quarters must be Very Good (VG) or better.
Note: Original wrapped rolls from 1968 to date command a small premium over spending value.
Note: No caribou circulation twenty-five cent coins were issued between 1997 and 2000.
Note: The Wheelchair Curling Mule is found only in the uncirculated sets of 2007.
Note: Coins must grade Very Good or better. Badly worn coins (good) will be priced lower.
Note: Original wrapped rolls from 1968 to date command a premium over spending value. Fifty cents 2002P to 2025 are issued only in rolls of 25, by the Royal Canadian Mint.
IMPORTANT: The silver dollar buying prices are for problem free coins in Very Fine (VF) condition. Damaged coins will bring lower prices.

DIE AXIS: The obverse design is considered the primary side of the coin. The die axis is the relationship of the reverse design to the obverse. Consider the obverse die, usually the anvil die in a press, stationary and when installed is the point of reference. The reverse die (moving hammer die) may be turned or set at any of 360 degrees in relation to the set obverse die. If the obverse die is identified by an upright arrow then the reverse die may be represented by a second arrow. These arrows form a relationship, illustrated, are two common die alignments. Coinage Axis: reverse die is set 180 degrees opposite. Medal Axis: reverse die is set in the matching direction.
Note: Refer to the previous page for Coinage definition.
